overview: CoStar Group is a leading provider of online real estate marketplaces, information, analytics, and 3D digital twin technology, built over 35+ years around the largest proprietary commercial real estate (CRE) research database and research department in the industry. The company operates in two segments -- Commercial Real Estate (CoStar Suite, LoopNet, STR hospitality benchmarking, Matterport, BizBuySell, Ten-X) and Residential Real Estate (Apartments.com, Homes.com, Land.com, Domain in Australia, OnTheMarket in the U.K., Zonda) -- restated from a geography-based structure in Q4 2025. It operates primarily in the U.S., with a growing presence in Australia, the U.K., Canada, and continental Europe, and has grown heavily through acquisition (Matterport, Visual Lease, Domain, Zonda, and a pending Vexcel deal) on top of organic subscriber growth.

business_model.summary: The majority of revenue (~93% in FY2025) comes from subscription-based license agreements, mostly auto-renewing with terms of at least a year and inflation-linked price escalators, sold to commercial and residential real estate professionals (CoStar Suite, LoopNet, Apartments.com, OnTheMarket). The remainder is transactional: Domain's premium listings in Australia, Matterport camera sales/capture services, and Ten-X auction fees (a percentage of the closing sale price). Acquisitions (Matterport, Domain, Zonda, Visual Lease) have driven a growing share of transactional/non-subscription revenue and most of the last two years' reported revenue growth.

Other Commercial Real Estate (Matterport, BizBuySell, Ten-X)
Residential Real Estate (Apartments.com, Homes.com, Land.com, Domain, OnTheMarket, Zonda)

business_model.customer_type: Primarily B2B subscription (brokers, agents, property owners/managers, landlords, lenders, appraisers, REIT managers) layered with B2C-facing marketplaces (consumers/renters/homebuyers use most sites for free; revenue comes from advertisers, agents and property managers). Revenue is described by the company as highly diversified with no material customer concentration.
business_model.geographic_mix: U.S. the large majority (~78% of ~8,000+ employees U.S.-based); international revenue (Australia via Domain, U.K. via OnTheMarket/CoStar UK, Canada, continental Europe) was approximately 14-15% of revenue in 2026, concentrated in GBP, AUD, CAD and EUR.

main_competitors: CREXi (CRE marketplace; active antitrust/copyright litigation with CoStar)
CoreLogic, Yardi, RealPage, MRI Software (CRE/multifamily data & software)
competitive_position.market_position: Dominant, long-entrenched #1 in commercial real estate information/analytics (CoStar Suite) and a top player in CRE listings (LoopNet) and apartment listings (Apartments.com); a distant and heavily-subsidized #2 in for-sale residential listings, where Homes.com's network averaged ~108 million monthly unique visitors in 2025 versus Zillow's ~235 million.

moat_factors.description: 35+ years of field-researched, standardized CRE data (hundreds of fields per property) collected by the industry's largest dedicated research staff; difficult and expensive for a new entrant to replicate.
CoStar Suite subscriptions are embedded in brokers'/lenders' daily workflows (comps, tenant data, debt solutions, lease analytics), producing historically high (though now softening) renewal rates.
LoopNet and Apartments.com benefit from two-sided scale (listings attract searchers, searchers attract advertisers), but Homes.com's residential network effect is still subscale versus Zillow.
CoStar and STR are widely viewed as the industry-standard data sources for CRE and hospitality benchmarking, respectively.

Balance sheet and cash flow have funded a steady stream of bolt-on acquisitions (Matterport, Visual Lease, Domain, Zonda, pending Vexcel) that extend the data moat into adjacent categories (3D digital twins, lease accounting, aerial imagery, homebuilder data).

weaknesses: Homes.com remains a distant, cash-burning #2 to Zillow on traffic and lead generation, with management not targeting standalone Homes.com profitability until 2030

Net new bookings have missed expectations for roughly five consecutive quarters and renewal rates have declined from ~92% (FY2021-era) to 88% (TTM Q3-2026), suggesting real competitive and sales-execution erosion, not just tough comparisons
Heavy and recurring reliance on M&A for growth (Matterport, Domain, Zonda, Vexcel) raises integration risk and has driven goodwill/intangibles to ~$7.5 billion
Ongoing litigation exposure: CREXi antitrust/copyright disputes, an STR hotel-benchmarking antitrust class action, and a Zillow copyright infringement suit against CoStar
Activist investor campaigns (Third Point, D.E. Shaw) in 2026 have forced strategic distraction and a sharp pullback in growth investment, which appears to have contributed to the bookings slowdown

growth_drivers: Homes.com scaling under the 'Your Listing, Your Lead' model, with price increases for new agent subscribers (effective May 2026) and depth-advertising/new-homes-builder product expansion
AI integration across the portfolio (Homes AI, Apartments AI, a planned CoStar AI) intended to improve conversational search, lead quality and internal research/data-collection efficiency
International expansion of LoopNet and CoStar into France, Spain and (planned) Australia, leveraging the Domain Acquisition's local footprint
Continued CoStar Suite module expansion (new homes data, valuation, lease and debt benchmarking) to drive incremental subscriber and usage revenue

Bolt-on M&A extending the data moat into adjacent categories: Matterport (3D digital twins), Visual Lease (SaaS lease accounting), Domain (Australian residential/commercial marketplaces), Zonda (homebuilder/residential-construction data and analytics), and the pending Vexcel acquisition (aerial/geospatial imagery, >$140 million TTM revenue growing >30% at ~20% EBITDA margin)

A sharp, ongoing reduction in Homes.com net investment (guided down more than $300 million in 2026 versus ~$850 million in 2025) is already driving large Adjusted EBITDA margin expansion if it can be sustained without further damaging bookings

business.description: Annualized net new bookings fell to $37 million in Q3 2026 from $84 million a year earlier (management cited 'economic headwinds and slower-than-expected sales force growth within a competitive environment'); the trailing-12-month renewal rate has slipped from ~90% (FY2023) to 88% (TTM Sept 2026) while the cancellation rate has risen to 12%.

Homes.com's ~108 million average monthly unique visitors in 2025 trail Zillow's ~235 million; management does not expect Homes.com to reach standalone positive Adjusted EBITDA until 2030, implying years of continued investment risk.

Matterport, Visual Lease, Domain, Zonda and the pending Vexcel deal must all be integrated simultaneously; goodwill and intangibles reached ~$7.5 billion as of Q3 2026, creating impairment risk if any underperforms.

Third Point and D.E. Shaw both publicly pushed in early 2026 for a Homes.com spin-off or sale; Third Point exited its stake in April 2026, but D.E. Shaw's stance (as of its last public letter) had not been resolved, leaving a governance overhang.

Founder/CEO Andrew Florance is explicitly flagged in filings as material to the business; a recent CFO transition (Robin Rossmann succeeding Christian Lown, effective July 31, 2026) adds near-term execution risk during a period of activist pressure and cost-cutting.

financial.risk: Cash depletion from M&A and buybacks
financial.description: Cash and equivalents fell from $1.7 billion (Dec 2025) to $500 million (Sept 2026) due to the Zonda acquisition, Richmond/Arlington campus construction, and $1.5 billion share-repurchase program; the pending $730 million Vexcel deal will draw further on cash/revolver.
Net interest income fell sharply (down ~48% in FY2025, down further in 2026) as cash balances used for acquisitions and buybacks shrank, removing a prior earnings tailwind.
Roughly 14-15% of revenue is denominated in AUD, GBP, CAD and EUR, unhedged, following the Domain acquisition's increase in Australian-dollar exposure.
$1.0 billion of Senior Notes outstanding plus a $1.1 billion undrawn revolving credit facility with a 4.50x net-leverage covenant; manageable today but a constraint on further large cash deals.

regulatory.description: Ongoing disputes with CRE marketplace competitor CREXi, including antitrust claims that CoStar monopolizes CRE information markets and a copyright case in which a federal court found CREXi infringed CoStar's images.

regulatory.risk: STR hospitality benchmarking antitrust class action
regulatory.description: A putative class action (filed Feb 2024) alleges STR's hotel-benchmarking data facilitated price coordination among hotel operators; CoStar is defending but cannot predict the outcome or loss, if any.
Zillow is litigating against CoStar over alleged photo/content copyright infringement tied to the Homes.com/Zillow rivalry.

A Delaware court ruled former Matterport CEO Bill Brown was entitled to recover damages tied to post-IPO share lockup restrictions; CoStar inherited the liability through the Matterport acquisition and paid roughly $109 million (including interest) in 2026 to settle.
The EU AI Act, DSA, Data Act, GDPR/CCPA, and evolving MLS rules all raise compliance costs and could restrict data access or AI feature deployment (e.g., Homes AI, CoStar AI).

macro.description: Elevated U.S. and Australian interest rates in 2026 have slowed real estate transaction volumes and raised inventory, directly cited by the company as a driver of weaker bookings and reduced Domain (Australia) transaction volumes.
Higher mortgage rates and slower home-sale activity reduce real estate agents' advertising budgets, pressuring Homes.com and Apartments.com monetization.

CoStar's own risk factors note that commercial real estate sectors (office, industrial, retail, multifamily) move through cycles with different timing, and a broad downturn would reduce subscriber/advertiser demand.

macro_factors.industry_outlook: Online real estate information, analytics and marketplace advertising remains a secularly growing category, but near-term volumes are constrained by elevated interest rates that have slowed both commercial real estate transaction activity and residential home sales in the U.S. and Australia.
macro_factors.cyclicality: Moderate; subscription revenue is relatively sticky, but net new bookings, listing volumes, and transactional revenue (Domain premium listings, Ten-X auctions) are sensitive to real estate transaction cycles and interest rates.
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Moderate-to-high indirect sensitivity: higher rates slow CRE and residential transaction volumes, which the company explicitly links to its 2026 bookings and Domain revenue softness; CoStar's own debt is largely fixed-rate, limiting direct balance-sheet sensitivity.
key_input_costs: Matterport hardware components (partly sourced from China, exposed to tariffs)

recent_developments.event: Completed the Matterport acquisition (3D digital-twin technology), funded largely with CoStar stock.
Completed the Domain Holdings Australia acquisition (A$4.43/share scheme of arrangement), adding Australia's leading residential/commercial marketplace.
Restated reportable segments from geography-based to product-portfolio-based (Commercial Real Estate / Residential Real Estate) to align with internal management reporting.

Issued FY2026 and medium-term outlook guiding to a net reduction in Homes.com investment of more than $300 million in 2026 (from ~$850 million in 2025) and significant Adjusted EBITDA expansion, with Homes.com standalone profitability not targeted until 2030.

Activist investors Third Point (Daniel Loeb) and D.E. Shaw publicly pushed CoStar to spin off or sell Homes.com, estimating over $10 billion of potential shareholder value unlock; stock hit new 52-week lows amid the campaign.
Third Point disclosed it had exited its entire CoStar position, stating it no longer believed its original activist thesis held.
Raised Homes.com subscription pricing for new agent customers as part of the monetization push.
Announced (May 28) and completed (August 21) the ~$789 million cash acquisition of Zonda, a residential-construction/homebuilder data and analytics provider.
Robin Rossmann (previously CoStar's Europe Managing Director) promoted to Chief Financial Officer effective July 31, 2026, succeeding Christian Lown, who departed for an external CFO role.
Q2 2026 earnings prompted a wave of analyst target cuts and a KBW downgrade to Market Perform on continued bookings softness, pushing the stock to a new 52-week/1-year low.

Q3 2026 results: revenue of $952 million (+14% YoY) beat consensus and Adjusted EBITDA more than doubled YoY (above the high end of guidance), but annualized net new bookings fell to $37 million from $84 million a year earlier -- roughly a fifth consecutive quarterly bookings miss -- and the trailing-12-month renewal rate slipped to 88%; the stock fell ~13-14% on the print and several analysts (including Goldman Sachs and BTIG) cut price targets despite raised full-year profit guidance.

Announced a definitive agreement to acquire Vexcel Group, a survey-grade aerial-imagery/geospatial data provider (>$140 million TTM revenue, growing >30%, ~20% Adjusted EBITDA margin), for approximately $730 million in cash, expected to close in H1 2027 pending HSR and other regulatory clearances.

guidance.management_commentary: Management has repeatedly framed 2026 as a deliberate pivot from growth investment to margin expansion -- cutting net Homes.com spend by over $300 million and pulling back sales-force hiring -- while characterizing Q3 2026 as the 'bookings trough.' It continues to resist activist calls (from D.E. Shaw, after Third Point's exit) to divest Homes.com, arguing a sale or spin-off would cause 'irreparable harm,' and points to Zillow's declining unique-visitor trend (down for 15 consecutive months per comScore data cited by CoStar) as evidence the 'Your Listing, Your Lead' strategy is gaining relative ground even as absolute scale remains far behind Zillow.

bull_case: Unmatched proprietary CRE database and research organization built over 35+ years gives the core CoStar Suite subscription business a durable, high-switching-cost moat with embedded pricing power

The 2026 cost discipline at Homes.com is visibly working in the numbers: Residential segment Adjusted EBITDA swung from roughly a $230 million loss to a $32 million profit over the first nine months of 2026 even as revenue kept growing, and full-year Adjusted EBITDA guidance has been raised twice

Large buyback authorization ($1.5 billion, with over $800 million still available) against a stock down roughly 65% from its 2026 highs gives management a cheap lever to return capital or buy back shares
Disciplined bolt-on M&A (Zonda, pending Vexcel) is extending the data/analytics moat into adjacent, faster-growing, higher-margin categories without abandoning the core subscription model

Activist pressure (even after Third Point's exit) has already forced management toward capital discipline, and the Homes.com spin-off/sale optionality that D.E. Shaw has proposed remains a potential catalyst for value realization
bear_case: The core growth engine shows real cracks: net new bookings have missed for roughly five consecutive quarters, and the subscription renewal rate has fallen from the low-90s% to 88% while cancellations have risen to 12%, suggesting the pullback in sales/marketing investment is damaging the franchise, not just smoothing margins

Homes.com remains a distant #2 to Zillow on audience scale (108 million vs. 235 million monthly unique visitors) with management's own timeline putting standalone profitability out to 2030 -- a long runway in which further cost cuts could permanently cede residential market share

A string of large, serial acquisitions (Matterport, Visual Lease, Domain, Zonda, pending Vexcel) has pushed goodwill and intangibles to roughly $7.5 billion and drained cash from $1.7 billion to $500 million in nine months, concentrating integration and impairment risk alongside inherited liabilities such as the ~$109 million Brown Judgment payment from the Matterport deal

Active litigation on multiple fronts -- CREXi antitrust/copyright disputes, an STR hospitality-benchmarking antitrust class action, and a Zillow copyright suit -- adds legal, reputational and potential monetary risk on top of normal operating risk

The stock's roughly 65% decline from 2026 highs reflects a genuine credibility problem: guidance has repeatedly been cut on bookings even as profit guidance is raised on cost cuts, a CFO transition is underway, and activist overhang (D.E. Shaw) persists even after Third Point's exit
